name: Shave your head

angle.text: Men with thinning or receding hair shave or clip their heads to replace a patchy look with a clean, deliberate one. Proponents say it reads as confident. The change is visible straight away, with mixed perception research and no clinical trials.

summary: Clip or shave down to embrace thinning hair; a style choice with mixed perception research and no clinical trials.
note: Perception studies on bald men conflict; sun protection for the scalp is commonly advised by dermatology bodies.
currentQuick:
Shaving the head means removing remaining hair to a short uniform length or smooth scalp, often as an alternative to concealing or treating hair loss. It has a long cultural history with religious, military, sporting and fashion meanings.
In appearance communities it is often presented as a clean, confident option for men with receding or thinning hair. Published research on how bald or shaved men are perceived is mixed.
How it works: Hair is cut with clippers or shaved with a razor. It does not change the underlying hair growth cycle or treat hair loss; it changes how the remaining hair and scalp appear.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks are minor: razor irritation or nicks and, for exposed scalp, sun exposure. No clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found.
deepLead:
Shaving the head is a style approach, discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a response to hair loss, in which a person with thinning or receding hair removes the remaining hair to a uniform short length or to the skin rather than trying to conceal or treat the loss. Proponents describe it as a way to present a deliberate, clean look instead of a partial one.
Head shaving has a long history across cultures, with records from ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and it carries varied meanings including religious practice, military uniformity, punishment, sport, solidarity with cancer patients and fashion. For men with pattern hair loss, encyclopedic sources list shaving the head as one way to improve the appearance of the condition, and note a proposed social theory that fully bald men may be read as signaling dominance or high status; survey results on how bald men are rated have differed between studies and cultures.
No clinical studies specifically testing head shaving as an appearance strategy were identified for this article, and sources on the topic are limited.

name: Stress and sleep management for hair

angle.text: People with diffuse shedding after a stressful period work on stress and sleep, hoping for less hair fall and recovery of density. It targets telogen effluvium. The mechanism is plausible, and it is untested as a hair treatment in people.

summary: Reducing stress and fixing sleep to ease shedding; plausible for telogen effluvium but untested as a hair treatment in people.
note: Shedding has many triggers; persistent shedding is generally evaluated by a clinician.
currentQuick:
This approach aims to curb diffuse shedding by addressing triggers such as stress, poor sleep, crash dieting or illness. The condition usually involved, telogen effluvium, is described as temporary, with hair regrowing over months.
Mouse and follicle studies suggest stress pathways can affect hair cycling, but no human trials were found testing stress or sleep programmes for hair outcomes.
How it works: Stress and other triggers are proposed to push growing follicles early into the resting phase, with shedding after about 2 to 3 months. Removing the trigger is described as allowing the cycle to normalise.
Risks and caveats: The approach itself carries little direct risk. Sources note that shedding can also reflect thyroid disease, nutrient deficiency or medications, so evaluation of persistent hair loss is generally advised by clinicians.
deepLead:
Stress and sleep management for hair refers to lifestyle approaches that people use to address diffuse hair shedding they attribute to stress, poor sleep or other triggers, most commonly the condition known as telogen effluvium. In telogen effluvium, a larger-than-usual share of scalp hairs shifts early into the resting (telogen) phase and sheds, typically a few months after a trigger.
Triggers described in medical sources include severe illness, surgery, childbirth, rapid weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, thyroid disease, some medications and emotional or psychological stress. The condition is usually described as temporary, with regrowth over months once the trigger resolves, and no specific drug is typically needed.
Laboratory work in mice found that psychoemotional stress can prematurely end hair growth and induce follicle inflammation through the neuropeptide substance P. Human evidence tying specific sleep or stress-reduction programmes to hair outcomes was not found for this article.

name: Inversion method / scalp stretching exercises

angle.text: Some hair-loss communities hang upside down or stretch the scalp, believing a looser scalp and better blood flow supports regrowth. Followers hope for thicker hair. No hair studies of these practices exist.

summary: Hang upside down or stretch the scalp to boost blood flow for hair; no hair studies exist, and inversion has cardiovascular and eye cautions.
note: Inversion is listed as higher-risk for people with heart disease, hypertension or glaucoma.
currentQuick:
These routines claim that inverting the body or stretching the scalp improves blood flow or reduces tension, supporting hair growth. They circulate in hair-loss forums as drug-free options.
No clinical studies testing either approach for hair growth were found.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is increased scalp circulation or reduced scalp tightness. Inversion therapy is otherwise a form of spinal traction.
Risks and caveats: Inversion raises heart rate and venous return and is listed as higher-risk for people with heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma, reflux or pregnancy. Scalp massage is generally low-risk.
deepLead:
Inversion methods and scalp stretching exercises are routines promoted in some hair-loss communities, based on the idea that loosening a tight scalp or increasing blood flow to it supports hair growth. They include hanging upside down on inversion tables or gravity boots, and manual scalp massage or stretching.
Inversion therapy itself is a form of spinal traction in which a person hangs by the ankles or feet. Encyclopedic sources describe its main benefit as short-term and pleasant, with no clinical trial results offered, and list heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma and pregnancy among conditions with higher risk.
No published clinical studies of inversion or scalp stretching for hair growth were found for this article.

name: Dermastamping with minoxidil

angle.text: Users stamp the scalp with microneedles before applying minoxidil, aiming for stronger regrowth and a denser look. It is a home variant of dermarolling. Small studies of microneedling plus minoxidil hint at added benefit, and the evidence is thin.

summary: Stamp the scalp with microneedles, then apply minoxidil; small studies hint at added benefit but evidence is thin.
note: Microneedling outside medical settings carries infection risks; minoxidil can irritate the scalp.
currentQuick:
Dermastamping is a microneedling variant in which a needled stamp is used on the scalp before topical minoxidil. Users say it improves absorption and stimulates follicles.
A small pilot study cited by Wikipedia found the combination more effective than minoxidil alone in androgenetic alopecia, but evidence is limited.
How it works: Microneedling creates tiny skin punctures, proposed to enhance drug delivery and trigger wound-healing growth factors. Minoxidil is converted to minoxidil sulfate and affects potassium channels and the follicle cycle.
Risks and caveats: Risks include skin irritation, shedding, and infection with poor hygiene; health agencies have warned of blood-borne infection risks from microneedling in non-medical settings.
deepLead:
Dermastamping with minoxidil is a hair-loss routine in which a person uses a microneedle stamping device on the scalp and applies topical minoxidil afterwards, on the idea that small skin punctures improve absorption or stimulate follicles. It is a variant of dermarolling.
Encyclopedic sources report that some studies found microneedling combined with minoxidil more effective than minoxidil alone, citing a small pilot study of androgenetic alopecia. A 2024 retrospective study of 230 people with alopecia areata examined microneedle application of minoxidil with triamcinolone, a different condition.
Safety concerns for microneedling are greatest in non-medical settings without infection control.

name: Low-dose finasteride microdosing

chain: Hair kept with fewer side effects
angle.text: Men with pattern hair loss use below-label finasteride amounts, hoping to hold their hairline and density while lowering side-effect risk. DHT data are suggestive. Trials on the lower amounts for hair are lacking.

summary: Taking below-label finasteride to cut side effects; DHT data are suggestive but trials on lower doses are lacking.
note: Off-label; finasteride carries label warnings on sexual and mood effects.
currentQuick:
Microdosing means using less finasteride than the labelled 1 mg hair-loss dose, in hope of lowering side effects while keeping hair benefits.
Pharmacology reports show DHT suppression is near-maximal at low doses, but trials comparing hair results and side effects across doses were not found.
How it works: Finasteride blocks type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, reducing DHT. A reported 0.2 mg dose lowered DHT 68.6 percent versus 72.2 percent at 5 mg.
Risks and caveats: Label warnings cover sexual dysfunction, depression and suicidal thoughts; the EMA confirmed suicidal thoughts in 2025. It is Rx-only and contraindicated in pregnancy. Whether lower doses reduce risk is unproven.
deepLead:
Low-dose finasteride microdosing is a practice in which men with pattern hair loss take finasteride in amounts below the 1 mg daily dose approved for hair loss, usually hoping to keep hair benefits while lowering the chance of sexual or mood side effects. Finasteride is a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as Propecia (1 mg) for hair loss and Proscar (5 mg) for benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Encyclopedic sources report that a 0.2 mg daily dose achieved near-maximal reduction of circulating DHT, 68.6 percent, compared with 72.2 percent at 5 mg. No large randomized trials establishing the hair efficacy or side-effect rates of lower-than-approved doses were identified for this article.
The practice is not a labelled use, and people considering it generally discuss it with prescribers.

name: Post-finasteride syndrome concerns

angle.text: Post-finasteride syndrome is a heavily discussed topic among men deciding whether to use finasteride to keep their hair. Posters debate how common persistent symptoms are and what causes them. It is not a formal diagnosis, and regulators have added warnings.

summary: The debate over persistent side effects after finasteride; regulators have added warnings but incidence and cause remain disputed.
note: Not a formal diagnosis; regulators have added warnings on persistent sexual effects and suicidal thoughts.
currentQuick:
Post-finasteride syndrome is a proposed condition of sexual, mood and cognitive symptoms reported to continue after stopping finasteride. It is not a recognised diagnosis, and incidence and causation are debated.
Regulators have added warnings: the FDA in 2012 on persistent sexual effects and the EMA in 2025 on suicidal thoughts.
How it works: Proposed explanations include lowered neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, epigenetic changes and androgen-receptor changes. None is established in humans.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include erectile dysfunction, low libido, depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation. No approved treatment exists, and evidence is limited to surveys and retrospective studies.
deepLead:
Post-finasteride syndrome (PFS) is a proposed condition in which sexual, psychological and physical symptoms are reported to persist after stopping finasteride, a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor used for male pattern hair loss and prostate enlargement. It is not recognised as a formal diagnosis in ICD or DSM, and its validity and incidence are debated.
Reported symptoms include low libido, erectile dysfunction, depression, anxiety, cognitive complaints and fatigue. The FDA updated finasteride labelling in 2012 to describe persistent sexual side effects, and the European Medicines Agency confirmed in 2025 that suicidal thoughts can occur. A 2019 BMJ editorial called the syndrome ill-defined and controversial, while other researchers consider it real.
In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, PFS concerns are a central debate shaping decisions on whether to use finasteride.

name: Hairline lowering surgery

angle.text: Hairline lowering moves the hairline forward to shorten a tall forehead and rebalance facial proportions. Published series are mostly in women with a congenitally high hairline. The new hairline is visible after healing, and the scar is the central debate.

summary: Scalp-advancement surgery that moves the hairline down to shorten a tall forehead; published series are mostly in women, and the scar is the central debate.
note: Published outcome series are mainly in women with stable hairlines; forum users who are men discuss scar visibility and future hair loss as the main concerns.
currentQuick:
Hairline lowering surgery, also called forehead reduction, is a procedure in which an incision is made along the hairline and the scalp is loosened and pulled forward, so the hair-bearing skin sits lower and the forehead looks shorter. It is described in the plastic surgery literature mainly for women with a naturally high hairline, and as part of facial feminization surgery for transgender women.
On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an option for people who feel a large forehead throws off facial proportions. Users compare it with hair transplants and with hairstyling, and a recurring theme is how visible the scar is and whether it suits men, who may go on to lose hair.
How it works: The surgeon makes an incision at or just in front of the hairline, releases the scalp from the underlying tissue, and advances it forward before closing the wound. Published reports describe different incision designs and ways of anchoring the advanced scalp, including sutures tunnelled through bone. A hair transplant over the scar is sometimes added afterwards to disguise it.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include a visible or widened scar, numbness, and the limits on how far the scalp can be advanced. Forum users also raise the concern that surgery on a hairline that is still receding may leave the scar exposed later. Published series are small and mostly retrospective, and mostly involve women, so outcomes in men are less well documented.
deepLead:
Hairline lowering surgery, also called forehead reduction or scalp advancement, is a cosmetic procedure that shortens the vertical height of the forehead by moving the hairline forward. A surgeon incises along the hairline, frees the scalp from deeper tissue, advances it and closes the wound . Surgeons have described it chiefly for women with a congenitally high hairline and as one component of facial feminization surgery .
Published reports on the operation are mainly case series and technique descriptions. A retrospective review of 29 women treated by one surgeon over 20 years measured photographs before and after surgery , and a series of 91 patients described bone-tunnelling suture fixation of the advanced scalp . Other reports cover forehead reduction in women and hair-transplant alternatives for Asian women with high foreheads .
In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who attribute a long forehead to hairline position. Users on looksmax.org describe both favourable results and concerns about scarring, and some argue it suits women better than men .

name: Nanoneedling / hair microneedle patches

angle.text: Hair-loss communities use the terms nanoneedling and microneedle patches for products said to deliver actives into the scalp for thicker hair. Dissolving microneedle patches are a real drug-delivery technology. No published trial reviewed here tests them for hair growth.

summary: Dissolving microneedle patches are a real drug-delivery technology, but no published trial reviewed here tests them for hair growth.
note: Published patch studies cover psoriasis, vaccines, insulin and growth hormone, not hair loss.
currentQuick:
Microneedle patches are small arrays of tiny needles, often made of dissolving material, that release a drug into the upper skin layers. The term is used in hair-loss circles for patches said to deliver actives such as minoxidil or growth-factor products to the scalp.
Published research on dissolving patches concerns other uses, such as psoriasis, vaccines, insulin and hormones. No published human trial among the sources reviewed tested a dissolving microneedle patch for hair growth.
How it works: Dissolving needles penetrate the outer skin layer, then dissolve and release their payload into the skin. Laboratory and small human studies of such patches have examined delivery depth, stability and skin reactions.
Risks and caveats: A small human study of placebo dissolving patches found them well tolerated, with only mild redness that resolved. Microneedling in general can cause redness, bleeding and, with non-sterile tools, infection. Safety data for scalp hair products specifically were not found.
deepLead:
Microneedle patches are arrays of microscopic needles, typically tens to a few hundred micrometres long, that pierce the outer skin and deliver a drug into it. Dissolving versions are made of water-soluble materials that dissolve in the skin, so nothing needs to be removed afterwards . Hair-loss communities use the terms nanoneedling or microneedle patches for products said to deliver actives to the scalp.
Published research on dissolving patches covers delivery of methotrexate for psoriasis in a preclinical model, human growth hormone, insulin in diabetic rats, influenza vaccine in a human study, and mRNA formulations . No study among those reviewed tested such a patch on hair growth. Wikipedia notes that the claim that microneedling may promote hair growth rests on weak sourcing .

name: Red light therapy for scalp

angle.text: Users wear light caps or use combs and panels on thinning areas, hoping for denser hair. It is an at-home, non-drug add-on to other treatments. Reviews report tentative benefit and call for better long-term trials.

summary: Low-level light caps, combs and panels aimed at thinning hair; reviews report tentative benefit but call for better long-term trials.
note: Reviews cite high risk of bias in many trials; some LLLT marketers have faced FDA action over unsupported claims.
currentQuick:
Red light therapy for the scalp uses low-power lasers or LEDs, in caps, combs, helmets or panels, with the aim of slowing hair loss or thickening hair. It is a form of low-level laser therapy, also called photobiomodulation.
Reviews summarised on Wikipedia range from little evidence (2012) to tentative benefit (2014, 2015, 2017), with a mixed review noting high risk of bias. Authors call for randomized and long-term trials.
How it works: Proponents say the light stimulates cell function and healing in follicles. The encyclopedia entry describes this as a proponents' claim whose effectiveness is still under investigation.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mild pain or skin irritation, and long-term effects are unknown. Eye protection is suggested for some devices. Response may vary by skin type, and consulting a dermatologist is suggested.
deepLead:
Red light therapy for the scalp applies low-power laser or LED light to the head in the hope of treating thinning hair, usually androgenetic alopecia. It belongs to low-level laser therapy, also known as cold laser therapy or photobiomodulation, which proponents say promotes healing and cell function though effectiveness is still under investigation .
Reviews of the hair-loss literature differ. A 2012 review found little evidence, 2014 and 2015 reviews found tentative benefit or mixed results with a high risk of bias, a 2017 review reported that 10 of 11 trials showed improvement, and a 2019 meta-analysis favoured lasers over LEDs . In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a gear option alongside minoxidil and finasteride.

name: Hair loss vaccine / peptides (BPC-157 for hair)

angle.text: BPC-157 and similar peptide stacks are promoted online for scalp healing and hair regrowth. Posters treat them as an experimental route to thicker hair. No human hair-growth trial was found, and BPC-157 is not approved for human use.

summary: Peptide stacks such as BPC-157 are promoted online for scalp claims, but no human hair-growth trial was found.
note: BPC-157 is not approved by any drug regulator for human use and is banned by WADA.
currentQuick:
BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from a protein in human gastric juice. It is discussed online for healing and, by some users, for scalp and hair claims.
Its published research is mostly in laboratory animals, with very limited human data, and the Wikipedia article on it does not mention hair.
How it works: Animal studies suggest cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory effects and possible faster tissue healing. How, or whether, this would affect hair follicles has not been established in published human work found.
Risks and caveats: It is not approved by any regulator for human use and has been on the WADA prohibited list since 2022. Health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient, and because it promotes blood vessel growth there is concern it could affect undetected cancers.
deepLead:
BPC-157, also called Body Protection Compound 157, is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids derived from a protein in human gastric juice. It was discovered by Predrag Sikirić of the University of Zagreb, with a first publication in 1993 . It is not approved by any drug regulatory agency for human use .
Research has been mostly in laboratory animals, suggesting cytoprotective, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, while human evidence is very limited . The encyclopedia article does not mention hair growth, and no human hair trial was found. Online discussion of peptide stacks for scalp claims is therefore untested.

name: Hairline tattoo

angle.text: Users get scalp micropigmentation to create the look of a closely shaved head or added density along a thinning hairline, and to conceal transplant scars. The visible change is immediate; sourcing is mostly industry and press, with no clinical trials found.

summary: Scalp micropigmentation tattoos tiny dots to mimic stubble or density along the hairline; sourcing is mostly industry and press, with no clinical trials found.
note: Poor hairline work can look unnatural; the pigment is described as permanent but removable with laser.
currentQuick:
A hairline tattoo, formally scalp micropigmentation (SMP), is a superficial cosmetic tattoo that mimics tiny hair follicles. It can recreate the look of a buzz cut on a bald scalp, add density to thinning areas, or draw in a hairline.
The Wikipedia article is a short stub that relies mostly on news and magazine sources, and no clinical trials were found.
How it works: Pigment is deposited into the epidermis and upper dermis, typically over three to four sessions of about two hours, with ink matched to hair colour. A patch test for ink allergy may be done first.
Risks and caveats: The article names an unnatural result from poor hairline work and possible ink allergies as the main risks, and says there are no scientific data on long-term effects, with the treatment described as permanent but removable by laser.
deepLead:
A hairline tattoo, more formally scalp micropigmentation (SMP) or hair tattoo, is a non-surgical, superficial cosmetic tattoo that creates the look of closely shaved hair on a bald scalp or adds apparent density to thinning areas . It is also used to conceal hair transplant scars and other scars on the head .
The hairline is described as one of the most crucial parts of the treatment, and poor work can look unnatural, though hairlines can be adjusted or touched up relatively easily . The Wikipedia article is a short stub, with several claims lacking citations and sources that are mainly news and magazine pieces .

name: Sulfate-free shampoo

angle.text: Sulfate-free shampoo is chosen by people who want gentler cleansing for hair that looks soft and shiny, especially colored or dry hair. The benefit is a marketing premise; no trials have tested appearance outcomes.

summary: Shampoo made without SLS/SLES sulfates; marketed as gentler, with no trials on appearance outcomes.
note: Cleaning power of sulfate alternatives is described as debated; no head-to-head appearance trials found.
currentQuick:
Sulfate-free shampoos leave out the common foaming detergents SLS and SLES and use other cleansers instead. They are marketed to people with sensitive scalps, dry or textured hair, or chemically treated hair.
Encyclopedic sources describe SLS as an irritant for some people but report no evidence of cancer risk at normal use. No clinical studies comparing sulfate and sulfate-free shampoos for hair appearance were found.
How it works: Shampoos clean by surfactants binding oil and dirt so they rinse away. Sulfate surfactants do this strongly and foam well; alternatives such as cocoyl glutamate or isethionate clean by the same principle, with the trade-offs in cleaning strength and foam that sources describe as debated.
Risks and caveats: Sulfate-free shampoos are ordinary cosmetics; contact allergy to any shampoo ingredient is possible. SLS can irritate skin and eyes in some people. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by regulators like the US FDA.
deepLead:
Sulfate-free shampoo is a shampoo formulated without the sulfate surfactants most common in conventional products, chiefly sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) and sodium laureth sulfate (SLES). Instead it uses other cleansing agents such as sodium cocoyl glutamate or sodium cocoyl isethionate.
Sulfate surfactants are widely used because they foam well and trap oil and dirt. Sulfate-free products are marketed as gentler cleansers, and the category is associated with people who have sensitive scalps, dry or textured hair, or chemically treated hair. Encyclopedic sources note that the cleaning performance of the alternatives is still debated, since each has its own trade-offs.
SLS is a detergent that removes oils from skin and can irritate skin and eyes, with sensitivity varying between individuals; a 2005 Cosmetic Ingredient Review report, as summarized on Wikipedia, found no evidence that SLS is carcinogenic and considered it safe for brief use followed by rinsing. No published clinical trial in the sources reviewed has compared sulfate-free and sulfate-containing shampoos for appearance outcomes.

name: Co-washing

angle.text: Users with dry, curly or textured hair co-wash to keep moisture in and cut frizz so curls look smoother and more defined. It is reported mainly through hair-care communities, and appearance outcomes are untested in trials.

summary: Washing hair with conditioner instead of shampoo; gentle for dry or curly hair, with buildup the reported trade-off.
note: Reviewed only in a narrative review; may leave residue buildup.
currentQuick:
Co-washing means cleansing hair with conditioner rather than shampoo. It is mostly used on dry, sensitive, chemically treated or curly hair.
A 2019 review describes it as gentle but prone to buildup, and sources note it cleans less thoroughly, so it is often alternated with a clarifying shampoo.
How it works: Cleansing conditioners use milder cleansing agents and conditioning ingredients, so they remove less oil and product than shampoo while coating the hair strand.
Risks and caveats: The main reported issue is residue buildup under the cuticle. Silicone-free formulations are generally described as preferred for co-washing. No safety concerns beyond ordinary cosmetic irritation are documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Co-washing, short for conditioner washing, is the practice of cleansing hair with a conditioner or a dedicated cleansing conditioner instead of shampoo. It is mainly associated with dry, sensitive, chemically processed or textured and curly hair.
A 2019 dermatology review describes co-washing as cleansing with a conditioner free of silicones, petrolatum and mineral oils, and reports that it is gentle on hair but may lead to buildup from residues under the cuticle scales. Wikipedia notes that cleansing conditioners clean less thoroughly than shampoo and are often alternated with a clarifying shampoo.

name: Olaplex bond builder

angle.text: Olaplex is used by people with bleached or heat-styled hair who want it to look and feel less damaged. The repair mechanism is described by the company; evidence in the sources is company-cited testing rather than independent trials.

summary: Brand-defining bond-repair hair treatment; widely sold, but only company-cited testing and a lawsuit history in the sources.
note: 2023 lawsuits allege hair damage and loss; the company disputes them.
currentQuick:
Olaplex is a hair-care brand that popularized bond-repair treatments, which are applied during or after bleaching and coloring to protect hair. Its patented active ingredient is bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate.
The company cites third-party testing and a 2024 review of the ingredient; the sources reviewed contain no independent clinical trials.
How it works: The stated mechanism is that the ingredient binds keratin and reconnects broken disulfide bonds within the hair, which chemical services and heat can sever.
Risks and caveats: A 2023 lawsuit by 28 women alleged hair damage and hair loss, and that older Lilial-containing formulas stayed on sale. Olaplex disputes the claims and cites third-party safety testing; a judge declined class treatment. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by regulators like the US FDA.
deepLead:
Olaplex is an American hair-care brand founded in 2014 whose products are marketed as repairing hair damaged by chemical, heat and mechanical stress. Its products contain a patented ingredient, bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate, which the company says reconnects broken disulfide bonds in hair.
The brand launched as a salon-only treatment used during bleaching and coloring, and later added retail products such as the No.3 treatment, No.4 shampoo and No.5 conditioner, creating the broader category of bond-repair or bond-building treatments. Wikipedia notes that a 2024 review of the ingredient describes how it reacts with keratin to restore hair bonds.
Olaplex has also been the subject of litigation, including a trade-secret dispute with L'Oreal and a 2023 lawsuit by women alleging hair damage and hair loss, which the company disputes. No independent clinical trials of bond-builder treatments appear in the sources reviewed.

name: Keratin smoothing treatment

angle.text: A salon keratin treatment is used to straighten frizz and add shine, with results visible right away and lasting a few months. Users choose it for a sleeker head of hair; the smoothing is the cosmetic effect itself.

summary: Salon keratin-and-heat smoothing for frizz and curl; lasts months, with formaldehyde exposure the documented concern.
note: Some formulations release formaldehyde; no appearance trials found.
currentQuick:
Keratin smoothing treatments are salon procedures that apply a keratin-based formula and seal it with a flat iron to reduce frizz and loosen curls for a few months.
The sources reviewed describe the effects and history but contain no clinical trials of appearance results.
How it works: Per Grokipedia, hydrolyzed keratin coats and fills the cuticle and heat seals it, mainly altering surface and hydrogen-bond interactions rather than permanently breaking disulfide bonds; formaldehyde-based versions rely on cross-linking.
Risks and caveats: Formaldehyde-releasing formulations can irritate eyes, nose and throat, and a 2014 study measured elevated formaldehyde in some products. Wikipedia advises against use during pregnancy. Overuse can cause dryness or breakage.
deepLead:
A keratin smoothing treatment, also called a Brazilian keratin treatment or Brazilian blowout, is a salon procedure in which a keratin-based solution is applied to hair and sealed in with heat, with the aim of reducing frizz, adding shine and loosening curl. Results are described as semi-permanent, typically lasting a few months.
Wikipedia groups keratin or Brazilian treatments with permanent and semi-permanent straightening methods and describes them as coating hair with keratin and then flat-ironing it, with effects fading over several months. Grokipedia says the method emerged in Brazil in the early 2000s and reached the United States around 2006.
The main documented concern is formaldehyde: a 2014 cross-sectional study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology examined formaldehyde concentrations in Brazilian keratin-type products, and a 2021 pilot study measured volatile organic compounds among hairdressers in salons serving women of color. Wikipedia advises against keratin treatments during pregnancy because some release gases.

name: Perm / texture perm

angle.text: Forum users get perms for added texture and volume, with posters claiming a boost of about 1 PSL and a way to cover weaker eye-area features. The curl change is visible at once; no attractiveness research backs the rating claims.

summary: Chemical waving/curling of hair; established salon procedure, popular in forums as a PSL boost with no attractiveness research.
note: Chemical process can damage hair and scalp; attractiveness effect untested.
currentQuick:
A perm chemically reshapes hair into waves or curls by breaking and reforming its disulfide bonds. Texture perms apply the idea for volume and a wavy or curly look.
Forum users claim perms raise looks ratings; no studies of that were found.
How it works: A reducing agent such as thioglycolate breaks keratin disulfide bonds while hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer, usually hydrogen peroxide, reforms them in the curled shape.
Risks and caveats: Chemical processing can irritate the scalp and damage hair, and related chemical relaxers are associated with burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss. Results grow out as new hair appears.
deepLead:
A perm (permanent wave) is a chemical hairstyling procedure that reshapes hair into waves or curls by breaking and reforming the disulfide bonds in keratin. A reducing agent, classically ammonium thioglycolate, breaks the bonds while the hair is wrapped on rods, and a neutralizer such as hydrogen peroxide reforms them in the new shape.
Modern perms descend from the 1938 cold wave, which required no heat, after earlier thermal and electric methods in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; types now include alkaline, acid, exothermic and digital perms. A texture perm refers to the use of such methods to add wave or curl for volume and texture.
On looksmaxxing forums, perms are discussed as a hair-based way to change facial framing; users there have claimed that a perm adds a point on the PSL scale. No published clinical studies of perms for attractiveness were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Hair relaxer / chemical straightener

angle.text: Relaxers are used to permanently straighten tight curls for a sleek, straight look, with new growth returning to natural texture. The straightening is visible straight away; cancer and fibroid links are under ongoing research.

summary: Alkaline chemical straightening of curly hair; effective cosmetically, with ongoing cancer and fibroid research and burn risks.
note: Observational studies link frequent use with uterine cancer; scalp burns are documented.
currentQuick:
Hair relaxers permanently loosen curls or straighten hair using alkaline or thioglycolate chemistry. New growth returns to its natural texture, so treatments are repeated.
Most research concerns health outcomes in Black women, where studies report differing findings across fibroids, breast cancer and uterine cancer.
How it works: The chemicals swell the hair shaft and break the disulfide bonds that hold its curl, so hair sets straighter.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include scalp burns, dermatitis, breakage and hair loss. Observational studies have linked frequent use to higher uterine cancer risk, and the FDA proposed banning formaldehyde in relaxers in 2023. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
deepLead:
A hair relaxer, or chemical straightener, is a cosmetic product that permanently loosens tight curls or straightens hair by breaking the bonds that hold its shape; new growth returns to its natural texture. Relaxers are almost always alkaline: lye relaxers use sodium hydroxide, and no-lye versions use other alkalis such as calcium, potassium or guanidine hydroxide, while others use thioglycolate or sulfite-based chemistry.
Early products date to 1909, when Garrett Augustus Morgan developed a straightening cream, with commercial lye relaxers appearing in 1917. Use is especially prevalent among Black women in the United States.
Research on health effects is active. Large cohort studies in the Black Women's Health Study examined relaxer use and uterine fibroids, breast cancer and uterine cancer, with differing findings, and the FDA proposed in 2023 to ban formaldehyde in hair relaxers.

name: Hair botox / hair filler treatment

angle.text: Hair botox is a marketing name for smoothing treatments that are promoted to cut frizz and add shine. The look is cosmetic and visible after application; the term has no fixed formula and no direct trials.

summary: A marketing name for protein-style smoothing treatments that promise less frizz and more shine; the term has no fixed formula and no direct trials.
note: Name is marketing; ingredients vary, and related smoothing treatments have drawn formaldehyde warnings.
currentQuick:
Hair botox, or hair filler, is a salon-style treatment sold to make dry, frizzy or damaged hair look smoother and shinier. Despite the name it is not an injection; the label is a marketing nickname.
It belongs to the same family as keratin and Brazilian smoothing treatments, which last weeks to months. No trials of products sold under this name were found.
How it works: Marketing says the products deposit protein or conditioning agents on the hair fibre to fill rough areas, often followed by heat styling. Encyclopedic sources note that hair is dead tissue, so cosmetics coat the fibre rather than repair it biologically.
Risks and caveats: Safety depends on the actual ingredients. Related smoothing treatments that contain or release formaldehyde have prompted warnings from regulators including the FDA, Health Canada and OSHA, and reported effects include eye and respiratory irritation. Regulation differs by country.
deepLead:
Hair botox, also marketed as a hair filler treatment, is the name given in the beauty industry to salon and at-home smoothing treatments that are described as depositing protein or conditioning agents on the hair to reduce frizz and add shine. The name borrows from injectable cosmetic procedures; it is a marketing term and has no single standard formulation.
The treatment sits in the same product family as keratin and Brazilian smoothing treatments, which use a smoothing solution sealed into the hair with a flat iron. Encyclopedic sources describe that family as lasting roughly two to six months . Some products in the wider family have drawn regulatory attention because of formaldehyde or formaldehyde-releasing ingredients , so the ingredient list of an individual hair botox product determines which safety information applies.
No published clinical trials of products sold specifically as hair botox or hair filler treatments were identified. Evidence about the category is limited to descriptions of related smoothing treatments and regulatory records.

name: Deep conditioner / hair mask

angle.text: People use a deep conditioner or hair mask on dry or damaged hair for softness and shine after a longer contact time. The improvement in feel and look is immediate but temporary, as these products coat the hair rather than repair it.

summary: A thicker, longer-contact conditioner for dry or damaged hair; it improves how hair feels and looks for now, but does not repair it.
note: Effects are cosmetic and wash out; mask ingredients such as egg can cause allergic reactions.
currentQuick:
A deep conditioner or hair mask is a richer conditioning product that stays on the hair for around 20 to 30 minutes after washing. It is used on dry, bleached, heat-styled or otherwise damaged hair to make it softer, shinier and easier to comb.
Encyclopedic sources say conditioners coat the hair rather than repair it, because hair is not living tissue. Claims of repair and strengthening are common in advertising but are not established in trials of the products.
How it works: Cationic surfactants bind to negatively charged hair and flatten the cuticle, fatty alcohols and silicones lubricate the fibre, and small proteins may enter the shaft. Heat is sometimes used to increase penetration.
Risks and caveats: Generally sold as a cosmetic. Allergic reactions to ingredients are documented, including a case report of food allergy triggered by an egg-based hair mask. Residue left on the scalp can flake.
deepLead:
A deep conditioner, also called a hair mask, is a thicker and more concentrated version of hair conditioner, applied after washing and left on for a longer period than ordinary rinse-out conditioner before being rinsed off. Wikipedia describes typical contact times of about 20 to 30 minutes and says these products are aimed at very dry or damaged hair .
Conditioners improve the feel, appearance and combability of hair mainly by reducing friction between fibres. Because hair consists of dead cells, they do not repair it biologically; they deposit material that coats the fibre and fills damaged areas of the cuticle . Benefits such as repair and strengthening are widely advertised, but the Wikipedia article treats them as claims rather than established outcomes .
No clinical trials of deep conditioners as a product category were located. Laboratory studies of individual conditioning ingredients exist and are summarised below.

name: Leave-in conditioner

angle.text: Leave-in conditioner is applied after washing for daily softness, detangling and frizz control. The smoothing effect is visible right away and temporary, and some formulas add heat protection.

summary: A no-rinse conditioner for daily softness, slip and frizz control; the effects are cosmetic and temporary.
note: Cosmetic coating only; buildup is reported if overused or applied to the scalp.
currentQuick:
A leave-in conditioner is applied to damp hair after washing and not rinsed out. It is meant to keep hair softer, smoother and easier to comb between washes, and some versions add heat protection.
It works on the surface of the hair, as encyclopedic sources say hair cannot be repaired biologically. No trials of the product category were found.
How it works: Light conditioning agents, usually cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants and oils, coat the fibre, flatten the cuticle, reduce friction and static, and leave a thin film that persists until the next wash.
Risks and caveats: Considered a low-risk cosmetic. Buildup and scalp flaking are reported with heavy use or application at the roots, and product guidance advises applying to lengths and ends. Individual ingredients can cause allergic reactions.
deepLead:
A leave-in conditioner is a no-rinse hair product applied to damp (or sometimes dry) hair after washing and left in. It is sold for ongoing moisture, detangling, smoothing, frizz reduction and, in some formulas, heat protection . Formats include creams, lotions, sprays and mists .
Wikipedia describes leave-in conditioners as lighter formulas than rinse-out types, often containing silicones or polymers, that reduce static and may offer some heat and UV protection . Conditioners in general improve combability and appearance by reducing friction between fibres; they coat the hair rather than repair it, since hair is not living tissue .
No clinical trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were found. Published research on conditioning agents is mostly laboratory testing of ingredients.
